opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it starts with understanding how the game works, because money is a game with rules, and most people were never taught them. So let me give it to you in the simplest terms I can.

First, you have to earn more than you spend. It sounds obvious, but that gap is everything. Even if it's a small amount, you want to save something, because savings give you two things: security and freedom. If you have about six months of living expenses set aside, you can handle a job loss or an emergency without being forced into a terrible position. If you get to a year or more, you have the freedom to make choices, to take a risk or retrain. So start there, even if it's only a little bit each month, and make it a habit.

Second, be careful about debt. Debt that lets you buy something that will produce more income, like an education that truly raises your earning power, can be good. Debt to fund consumption is a trap, because you're borrowing from your future self and paying interest for the privilege.

Third, don't keep your savings in cash for the long run. Cash feels safe, but it's actually one of the worst investments over time, because inflation quietly takes away its buying power. Put it into a well-diversified mix of assets, such as stocks, bonds, and some gold, across different countries and asset classes. The biggest mistake people make is thinking that the things that have done well recently are good investments rather than expensive ones. They buy high, get scared, and sell low. You're probably not going to beat the market by trading, because that's a zero-sum game against very skilled people. So don't try to time it. Diversify well, keep your costs low, and let compounding work over decades.

But the most important investment, especially when you have no money, is in yourself. Your earning power is your biggest asset at that stage. So build skills that people value, ones that will hold up in a world being changed by technology and AI. And surround yourself with good people, because who you learn from makes an enormous difference.

Finally, know that you will make mistakes and experience pain along the way. Everyone does. I went broke in 1982 and had to borrow $4,000 from my dad to pay my family bills. It was one of the best things that ever happened to me, because it taught me humility and how to diversify. Pain plus reflection equals progress. If you learn from your mistakes and keep improving, you can go a long way, no matter where you start.

r001.rationale: The response says that when someone has no money, “your earning power is your biggest asset at that stage.”

r002.rationale: It mentions technology and AI changing the world, but does not say that AI and machine automation productivity gains can widen income inequality.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes building valuable skills and earning power, but does not state that an individual's income is largely tied to their productivity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I've been there. I started with nothing. My dad was a jazz musician, my mother was a stay-at-home mom, we lived in a middle-class neighborhood on Long Island, and I caddied for a dollar a bag. So I don't say this from some lofty place. I say it as somebody who had to figure it out.

And the most important principle is very simple, almost boring: you have to spend less than you earn. That's the whole game at the start. Not the stock market, not clever investing. Spending less than you earn and saving the difference. Because savings equals freedom. When you have savings, you have the ability to say no, to take a risk, to survive a setback. When you don't, you're a slave to whatever's in front of you.

And the way I think about it is in terms of time. Calculate how many months you could live if you lost your income tomorrow. That number is your security. Most people have no idea what that number is, and for a lot of them it's close to zero. So the first goal is to build that up. Six months, a year, whatever you can get to.

The second thing is that your greatest asset, when you have no assets, is you. Your ability to earn. So the best investment you can possibly make at that stage is in your own earning power. Learn skills that are valuable, get around people who are better than you, and most importantly, learn from your mistakes. I've always said pain plus reflection equals progress. Every painful mistake I made, when I stopped and asked, "What does this teach me?", it made me better. That compounds in a way that's much more powerful than any interest rate.

And then third, once you've got that cushion, once you're saving, you can begin to invest, but you have to be humble about it. The biggest mistake people make with little money is they think they have to swing for the fences. They want the thing that'll make them rich fast. And in the markets, the thing that most people are sure will happen is very often the thing that doesn't, because it's already priced in. I nearly lost everything in 1982 because I was so certain I was right. That humility, learning to diversify so that no single bet can knock you out, that's what kept me alive.

So: spend less than you earn, build up the months of security, invest in your own capabilities, and then when you invest money, diversify and don't bet on being right. It's not exciting. But people who follow it almost always end up fine, and people who don't almost always end up in trouble.

r001.rationale: It calls the person’s ability to earn their greatest asset when they have no assets.

r002.rationale: It does not mention AI, machine automation, or their effect on income inequality.

r003.rationale: It recommends building earning power but does not state that income is largely tied to productivity.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by separating two things: earning more than you spend, and making what you save work for you.

If you have very little money, your first investment may need to be in your ability to earn. What skill can you develop that somebody will pay for? And can you develop it without taking on a lot of debt? At the same time, understand exactly where your money goes. Saving gives you a buffer, and that buffer gives you choices when something goes wrong.

Once you have some savings beyond what you need for emergencies, you can begin investing gradually. Be diversified, keep costs low, and don’t borrow money to make a bet you can’t afford to lose. You don’t have to predict the next great investment to make progress.

None of that guarantees security. And when your income barely covers necessities, cutting spending alone won’t solve the problem. But the direction is the same: build your earning power, create a surplus when you can, and protect it from a loss that could put you back at zero.

r001.rationale: The response recommends investing in earning ability, but does not identify a person’s earning capacity as their principal asset.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI, machine automation, or their effect on income inequality.

r003.rationale: The response discusses developing paid skills and building earning power, but does not state that income is largely tied to productivity.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with the relationship between what you earn and what you spend. If you can earn more than you spend and save the difference, even a small amount, you begin to give yourself options.

But when you have very little money, your greatest asset is your ability to learn and increase your earning power. Develop a skill that people need. Find people you can learn from. Think of that as an investment in yourself.

Then build a cushion, because unexpected things will happen, and you don’t want one setback to force you into expensive debt. As you accumulate savings, learn how to invest and diversify. Don’t assume that whatever has done well recently will keep doing well, and don’t risk money you need to live on.

There’s no guaranteed shortcut. But improving your earning power, keeping your spending manageable, and consistently putting something aside—that’s a foundation you can build on.

r001.rationale: It identifies the person’s ability to learn and increase their earning power as their greatest asset when they have little money.

r002.rationale: It does not mention AI or machine automation widening income inequality.

r003.rationale: It discusses increasing earning power but does not state that income is largely tied to productivity.
